\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{भयंकरः} (bhayaṅkaraḥ)}{भयंकरः (bhayaṅkaraḥ)}]{\sk{भयंकरः} (bhayaṅkaraḥ) — terrible}

\label{lesson:SA-C128-bhayankarah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for famous, then the Sanskrit for safe.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{भयंकरः}}
\textbf{\sk{भयंकरः}} — \emph{bhayaṅkaraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}terrible\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{bhayaṅkara} is built from \emph{bhaya} \textquotedblleft{}fear\textquotedblright{}, from the root √bhī \textquotedblleft{}be afraid\textquotedblright{} (MW), and \emph{-kara} \textquotedblleft{}making\textquotedblright{}, from √kṛ \textquotedblleft{}do, make\textquotedblright{}, with an \emph{ṃ} between them: \textquotedblleft{}fear-making\textquotedblright{}, so \textquotedblleft{}terrible\textquotedblright{} (MW).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bhayaṅkaraḥ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bhayaṅkaraḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{bhayaṅkaraḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for famous, then the Sanskrit for safe, then say \emph{bhayaṅkaraḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{मिथ्या} (mithyā)}{मिथ्या (mithyā)}]{\sk{मिथ्या} (mithyā) — false}

\label{lesson:SA-C128-mithya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for safe, then the Sanskrit for terrible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{मिथ्या}}
\textbf{\sk{मिथ्या}} — \emph{mithyā} — \textquotedblleft{}false\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mithyā} is an old adverb, \textquotedblleft{}invertedly, wrongly\textquotedblright{}, and later \textquotedblleft{}falsely\textquotedblright{}: MW contracts it from \emph{mithūyā}, and CDIAL 10130 sets it under the root √mith \textquotedblleft{}alternate, clash\textquotedblright{}. It lives on as Bengali \emph{michā} \textquotedblleft{}untrue\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 10130).
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{कटुः} (kaṭuḥ)}{कटुः (kaṭuḥ)}]{\sk{कटुः} (kaṭuḥ) — pungent}

\label{lesson:SA-C128-katuh}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for terrible, then the Sanskrit for false.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{कटुः}}
\textbf{\sk{कटुः}} — \emph{kaṭuḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}pungent\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{kaṭu} \textquotedblleft{}pungent, sharp, bitter\textquotedblright{} is old, in the Rigveda; MW tentatively links it with √kṛt \textquotedblleft{}cut\textquotedblright{}, but its origin is uncertain, and DEDR 1135 compares a Dravidian word. It lives on as Marathi \emph{kaḍū} and Hindi \emph{kaṛuā} \textquotedblleft{}bitter, pungent\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 2641).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{अम्लः} (amlaḥ)}{अम्लः (amlaḥ)}]{\sk{अम्लः} (amlaḥ) — sour}

\label{lesson:SA-C128-amlah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for false, then the Sanskrit for pungent.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अम्लः}}
\textbf{\sk{अम्लः}} — \emph{amlaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}sour\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{amla} \textquotedblleft{}sour, acid\textquotedblright{} appears from Manu on, and MW gives no derivation for it, so its origin is uncertain. It lives on as Bengali \emph{āmbal} \textquotedblleft{}sour\textquotedblright{} and Pali \emph{ambila} (CDIAL 579).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{तिक्तः} (tiktaḥ)}{तिक्तः (tiktaḥ)}]{\sk{तिक्तः} (tiktaḥ) — bitter}

\label{lesson:SA-C128-tiktah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for pungent, then the Sanskrit for sour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तिक्तः}}
\textbf{\sk{तिक्तः}} — \emph{tiktaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}bitter\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tikta} \textquotedblleft{}bitter, pungent\textquotedblright{} comes from the root √tij \textquotedblleft{}be sharp\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5806): bitterness as a sharp taste. MW compares √tij with Greek \emph{stizō} \textquotedblleft{}prick\textquotedblright{} and Latin \emph{distinguo}, and it lives on as Bengali \emph{titā} \textquotedblleft{}bitter\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5806).
\end{cousinweb}
